en: The summary verse concerning the person (*pudgalavastu*) is as follows:
Udāyin, the physical form, the limit, and furthermore, that which occurs later as the final one.
The summary verse:
Udāyin, by another, they remember, ashamed, now I know; the two-by-two performed;
Sudatta, Durdatta—the fourfold speech; through loss of mindfulness, four types are revealed.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery. At that time, Udāyin had committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense arising from the intentional emission of semen, which he had concealed for half a month.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, grant to the monk Udāyin, for this saṃghāvaśeṣa offense arising from intentional emission of semen and concealed for half a month, a half-month period of parivāsa."
Thus, or whoever else is of a similar kind;
furthermore, another person has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that was not concealed.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, grant this person a six-night *mānāpya* for this *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that has not been concealed."
Or whoever else is of a similar kind:
furthermore, another person has fallen into a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense;
he does not recognize those two offenses for two months.
After two months had passed, having concealed [the offense] for two months, he informs one group of monks and does not inform the other.
The Saṃgha granted him two months of parivāsa.
While still undergoing that parivāsa, he confessed that other offense which he had not previously announced in the midst of the Saṃgha.
He then informed the monks of this matter.
The monks [inquired] of the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"O monks, you should grant that person a *parivāsa* of exactly those same two months for his offense."
Or whoever else is of such a kind;
as he professes, so he remembers.
Now, another person has committed two offenses involving a formal meeting of the Saṃgha (saṃghāvaśeṣa).
He did not recognize those two offenses for two months;
having recognized them after the two months had passed, he concealed one offense for two months and then informed the monks of it,
while failing to inform them of the other.
The Saṃgha granted him two months of parivāsa.
While he was undergoing that parivāsa, being modest, he entered the Dharma.
He then informed the monks of this matter.
Venerable sirs, I have committed two offenses involving a formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṃghāvaśeṣa).
For two months I was unaware of those two offenses;
after two months had passed, having become aware of them and concealed them for two months, I now inform the monks of one of them.
The Saṃgha granted me two months of parivāsa.
Being one undergoing parivāsa, I was ashamed and fell away from the Dharma.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Bhikṣus, grant that person a period of probation (parivāsa) for that offense according as it was concealed;
or whoever else is of such a kind."
Just as he knows, so does he remember.
Now, suppose another person has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense;
while the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* is being recited for half a month, he says: "Now, venerable ones, I know that this rule is included in the Sūtra and contained within the Sūtra."
If the monks should know that this venerable one has previously sat for two or three poṣadha ceremonies, let alone more,
there is no release for that venerable one on account of ignorance.
He must be made to deal with that offense he has committed according to the Dharma.
Furthermore, he should be inspired with a sense of urgency;
he remembers exactly as he knows.
Now, there is another person who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

While the recitation of the Prātimokṣa-sūtra was being performed for half a month, he said: "Now, venerable ones, I know that this rule is included in the Sūtra and comprised within the Sūtra. If, monks, they do not know him—that this venerable one has previously attended two or three Poṣadha ceremonies, let alone more—there is no escape for that very venerable one on account of his ignorance.
Whatever offense he has committed, he should be made to deal with it according to the Dharma;
he should remember it just as he knows it.
Now, another person commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense;
he does not recognize it for one month.
Having recognized it after the lapse of that month, and having concealed it for one month, he informs the monks.
The Saṃgha granted him a two-month parivāsa.
While he was undergoing that parivāsa, he informed the monks who arrived one after another:
"Venerable sirs, I have fallen into a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense."

I, having fallen into that offense, recognized it; having recognized it after the lapse of one month, I concealed it for one month and then informed the monks. The Saṃgha granted me two months of parivāsa.
"Venerable ones, one month was well-granted, and one month was ill-granted."
For what reason?
Because it is contrary to the nature of things (*adharmatva*) and because the action is subject to agitation;
as he knows, so he remembers.
Now, another person commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense;
he does not recognize that offense for one month.
Having recognized it after the lapse of the month, and without concealing it, he informs the monks.
The Saṃgha granted him a month’s parivāsa.
He announced to the monks who arrived one after another:
"Venerable sirs, I have fallen into a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense."
Thus, I did not recognize that offense for one month;
having recognized it after the lapse of the month, I disclosed it to the monks without concealment.
The Saṃgha has granted me a month’s parivāsa for that.
"Venerable sir, it was wrongly given; it was not rightly given.
Why is that?
Venerable sir, it is one who deserves the *mānāpya* penance."
Just as he knows, so does he remember.
Now, another person has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; thinking, "I shall confess it after it has been concealed," he does not remember it.
Having remembered that offense and not concealing it, he informs the monks.
The monks [inquired] of the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"O monks, you should grant that person *parivāsa* for both continuities—that of the previous offense and that of the subsequent one—regarding that particular offense."
Or again, any other person of a similar kind:
suppose another person has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and, intending "I will confess it once it has been concealed," does not remember it;
having remembered it, he confesses it to the monks without concealing it.
The monks informed the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, you should grant that person *parivāsa* for the continuity of his previous offense."
Or whoever else is of a similar kind:
furthermore, another person who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, thinking "I shall confess it without concealment," does not remember it;
having remembered it, he conceals it and then informs the monks.
The monks [inquired] of the Blessed One;
the Blessed One said:
"O monks, grant that person parivāsa for that previous offense."
Or whoever else is of a similar kind:
furthermore, another person who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, thinking "I shall confess it without concealment," does not remember it;
having remembered it, he reports it to the monks without having concealed it at all.
The monks [inquired] of the Blessed One;
the Blessed One said:
"Monks, you should grant that person a *mānāpya* of six nights for that offense."
Or whoever else is of such a kind. Summary verse:
By height, sixteen; two, five, and twenty-eight.
By threes, there are three groups of eight; by fours, four groups of eight.
Three groups of eight were set aside, while five were proclaimed as the primary ones.
Now, another person, having committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that was concealed, went away;
having returned, he was ordained again.
Having concealed that very same offense, he informs the monks.
The monks [inquired] of the Blessed One;
the Blessed One said:
"O monks, grant that person parivāsa for that offense from both continuums."
Or whoever else is of a similar kind:
furthermore, another person has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, concealed it, and then wandered away;
he returns and is ordained once again.
Without concealing that offense, he informed the monks;
the monks [informed] the Blessed One;
the Blessed One said:
"Monks, you should grant that person parivāsa for the continuity of that previous offense," or whoever else is of a similar kind. Furthermore,
another person has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, which was not concealed, and he has gone away.
Having returned, he was ordained once again;
having concealed that offense, he informed the monks,
and the monks [informed] the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Bhikṣus, you should grant that person parivāsa for the continuity of that offense from its last occurrence;
or whoever else is of such a kind."
Now, there was another person who had committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that was not concealed; having left the community, he returned and was ordained again.
Without concealing that offense, he informed the monks of it.
The monks [inquired] about this matter of the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, you should grant that person a *mānāpya* (probation) for six nights for that offense."
Or whoever else is of this same class:
as there are four [results] for one who knows thus by means of the pure [meditation],
so there are four for one who remembers.
There are four [cases] involving doubt;
by this same method, there is another set of four,
though with a difference in the abbreviated formula (*peyāla*).
Furthermore, another person should be described as being "in the state of probation" (*pārivāsika*).

Just as with one who is in the state of probation, so too should those who have completed their probation (*paryuṣitaparivāsa*), those undergoing the *mānāpya* penance (*mānāpyacārika*), those who have finished the *mānāpya* (*caritamānāpya*), and those to whom a disciplinary training has been given (*śikṣādattaka*) be applied to the fourfold classification.
Just as with one who has gone astray, so too should one who claims to be a novice monk (*śramaṇoddeśaka*) be treated.

One should apply this in detail as follows: [the cases of] being insane, having a distracted mind, being overwhelmed by pain, being suspended for not seeing [an offense], being suspended for not making amends, and being suspended for not relinquishing an evil view.
Now, there is another person who has committed two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses—one concealed and one unconcealed—and has gone away.
Having returned, he was ordained once again.

Whatever offense he had concealed while he was wandering in confusion, that very same offense he now conceals when reporting it to the monks; and whatever offense he had not concealed, that too he now conceals when reporting it to the monks.
The monks [inquired] of the Blessed One;
the Blessed One said:
"O monks, grant that person *parivāsa* for both of his continuums."
"Of the first [period] and of the second,
the latter"— or whoever else is of such a kind.
Furthermore, another person has committed two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, one concealed and one unconcealed, and has then gone away.
Having returned, he was ordained once again.
He reported to the monks that very offense which he had previously concealed while wandering in distraction, without concealing it this time;
and he reported to the monks that offense which he had not previously concealed, likewise without concealing it.
The monks [inquired] of the Blessed One;
the Blessed One said:
"O monks, you should grant that person parivāsa for the continuity of his one previous offense."
"For one [offense] of the later category, there is a *mānāpya* for six nights"—
this applies to anyone else of a similar kind.
Furthermore, another person commits two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, one concealed and one unconcealed, and then goes away.
Having returned, he was ordained once again;
he then informed the monks that he had not concealed that [offense] for which he had previously wandered about in concealment,
but that he had concealed that which he had previously not concealed.
The monks [inquired] of the Blessed One;
the Blessed One said:
"O monks, grant that person parivāsa for the continuity of his one previous offense."
"Parivāsa for one [night] of the later period," or whatever other person of a similar kind there may be.
Furthermore, another person commits two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, both concealed and unconcealed, and then becomes confused.
Having returned, he was ordained once again.
That offense which he had concealed while he was wandering in confusion, he now fails to conceal and declares it to the monks;
however, that offense which he had not concealed, he likewise fails to conceal and declares it to the monks.
The monks [inquired] of the Blessed One;
the Blessed One said:
"O monks, you must give [it] to that single individual."
For the continuity [of offenses] prior to the offense, there is a *parivāsa*; for one subsequent offense, there is a six-night *mānāpya*. Or whoever else is of this same category.

Furthermore, another person who is a *pārivāsika*, one whose probation has been completed (*paryuṣitaparivāsa*), one undergoing the *mānāpya* penance, one who has completed the *mānāpya*, and one to whom the *śikṣādattaka* discipline has been granted,

should be addressed in the same manner as one who is "perplexed" (*vibhrānta*). Likewise, it should be said of one who claims to be a novice monk (*śramaṇoddeśaka*), or one who claims to be insane (*unmattaka*).
One should explain in detail: being of distracted mind, being of distinct feelings, being suspended for not seeing [the offense], and being suspended while having not renounced evil views.
Now, suppose another person has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, which was concealed for a limited duration.
He was suspended by the Saṃgha for not seeing [his offense].
Having been reinstated, he concealed those offenses and informed the monks;
the monks [informed] the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said: "O monks, you should grant that person *parivāsa* for those offenses, considering them to have a definite measure, for both continuities— both the prior and the subsequent—
and likewise for any other person of a similar kind."
Now, another person commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; it was concealed for a limited period.
He was then suspended by the Saṃgha for not recognizing [the offense].
Having been reinstated, he, without concealing those offenses, informs the monks;
the monks inform the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, you should grant that person a *parivāsa* (probation) for his previous continuity of offenses, considering those offenses to be of determinate measure;
or whoever else is of such a kind.
Furthermore, another person has fallen into a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
They were of measurable duration and not concealed.
He had been suspended by the Saṃgha for non-seeing,
and having been reinstated, he [confessed] those offenses.
Having concealed it, he informed the monks;
the monks [informed] the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, you should grant that person *parivāsa* for those offenses, considering them to have a definite measure, based on his subsequent continuity;
or whoever else is of such a kind.
Furthermore, another person commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
They were of measurable duration and not concealed.
He had been suspended by the Saṃgha for non-seeing;
having been reinstated, he, without concealing those offenses, informed the monks.
The monks [inquired] of the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, you should grant that person a *mānāpya* for six nights, considering those offenses of his to be of determinate measure."
Or whoever else of a similar kind;
as there are eight cases for those who have been suspended for [the offense of] "one who has a measurable amount," so too for those who have been suspended for "one who has no measurable amount";
as there are eight for one suspended for not seeing [the offense], so too for one suspended for not making amends; and as there are eight for one suspended for not renouncing a wicked view.
A person undergoing parivāsa committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and wandered away.
Having returned, he was ordained once again.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Let him undergo the parivāsa probation even though it has not yet been completed;
he shall become one whose parivāsa is completed."

Just as with one who is deranged, so too does one claim the status of a novice monk (*śramaṇoddeśaka*), or one who is insane, or one whose mind is distracted, or one overwhelmed by pain, or one who has been suspended for not seeing [an offense], or one who has been suspended for not making amends.
A person who, having completed his probation (*paryuṣitaparivāsa*) after committing a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, is then deranged; [in such cases, he may claim the status of a novice].
Having returned, he was ordained once again.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"O monks, this person has indeed completed his parivāsa;
let mānāpya be granted to him.
Just as with one who has wandered away, so too does he claim the status of a novice (śramaṇoddeśaka).
The same sequence as before applies, up to the case of one who has been suspended for not relinquishing an evil view.
A person undergoing the *mānāpya* penance commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and departs. Having returned, he is ordained once again.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Let him practice what has not been practiced."
"He shall have completed his *mānāpya*," as was previously stated regarding one who has gone astray;
this is the same abbreviated formula.
A person who had completed the *mānāpya* penance committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and went away.
Having returned, he was ordained again.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, this monk has indeed performed the mānāpya penance;
expel him."
As before, it is just as in the case of one who has become confused;
this is the same formula.
A person who has been suspended for not seeing [his offense] commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that is unconfessed.
He was suspended by the Saṃgha for not seeing [his offense].
Having been reinstated, he concealed that offense and informed the monks.
The monks [informed] the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Bhikṣus, you should grant that person parivāsa for the remainder of the continuity of that offense;
or whoever else is of such a kind."
A person who had been suspended for not recognizing [his offense] committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that was not concealed.
He was suspended by the Saṃgha for not recognizing it.
Having been reinstated, he—without concealing that offense—announced it to the monks.
The monks [inquired] about this to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said: "Monks, you should grant that person a six-night *mānāpya*."
Or whoever else is of this same category:
as there are two cases for one who knows by means of a pure [act], so there are two for one who remembers, and two for one who is in doubt.

As there are eight cases for one suspended for not confessing [an offense] according to what was seen, so there are eight for one suspended for not making amends, and eight for one suspended for not relinquishing an evil view.
The summary verse:
By way of the limit, there are the twelve-fold, the nine-fold, and those pertaining to all times;
having established the watchful nine-fold, there are fifteen steps.
Now, another person has committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense that is immeasurable and concealed;
he knows the limit of those offenses in terms of their occurrence, but not the limit in terms of the nights they have been concealed.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, you should grant that person the *aparimāṇavatī* [formal act] for those offenses."
Having thus performed the *parivāsa* for the inner quarters,
or whoever else is of a similar kind;
furthermore, another person has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
They concealed their offenses, which were immeasurable in number; he knew the duration of those nights, but not the extent of the offenses. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One said: "O monks, grant that person a period of probation (*parivāsa*) for those offenses, treating them as being of immeasurable duration (*aparimāṇavatya*), according to how long they were concealed."
Or whoever else is of such a kind;
furthermore, another person has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense,
which was concealed for an immeasurable period.
He did not know either their limit of offenses or the limit of the night.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One,
and the Blessed One said:
"Monks, you should grant that person a *śuddhāntika* probation, considering those offenses of his to be immeasurable (*aparimāṇavatya*).
This applies to whoever else is of such a kind.
Furthermore, there is another person who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
They concealed their offenses for an immeasurable duration. He knew the limit of those offenses as being the limit of the nights.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"O monks, grant that person *parivāsa* for those offenses, considering them to be of immeasurable duration, according to how they were concealed;
or whoever else is of such a kind."
Just as there are four [cases] for one who knows, so too there are four for one who remembers, and four for one who is doubtful.
Now, another person has committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and concealed it;
the Saṃgha has granted him *parivāsa* by means of an illegal act—one that is contested and subject to suspension.
While still undergoing the *pārivāsa* probation, he committed another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, an intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*) similar in form to his previous offense, which was concealed.

The Saṃgha granted him a *mūlaparivāsa* by means of an illegal act—one that is contested and subject to suspension. While still undergoing that *mūlapārivāsa*, he committed yet another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, a secondary intermediate offense (*pratyantarāpatti*) similar in form to the intermediate offense, which was also concealed.
The Saṃgha granted him a *mūlāpakarṣa* by means of an illegal act that was reversible and subject to suspension; it also granted him a *mānāpya* illegally,
and it also restored him illegally.
This person is called one who is impure at all times and has not emerged from that offense; he is not liberated from it.
Now, there is another person who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and concealed it.
The Saṃgha has granted him *parivāsa* by means of a formal act (*karma*) that is legal, irreversible, and not subject to suspension.
While still in the state of being on *pārivāsa*, he committed another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, an intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*) similar to his previous offense, which was concealed.
The Saṃgha granted him a *mūlaparivāsa* by means of an illegal act—one that is contested and subject to suspension.

While still in the state of being on *mūlapārivāsa*, he committed yet another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, a subsequent intermediate offense (*pratyantarāpatti*) similar to the intermediate offense, which was also concealed.
The Saṃgha granted him a *mūlāpakarṣa* by means of an illegal act— one that is reversible and subject to suspension—
and likewise a *mānāpya* by means of an illegal act,
and even a *āvrīḍha* by means of an illegal act.
This is called a person who is "mostly black" (*yadbhūyaskālaka*); he is impure, has not emerged from that offense, and is not liberated from it.
Now, another person commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and conceals it.
The Saṃgha grants him a period of probation (*parivāsa*) by means of a legal act that is irreversible and not subject to suspension.
While still undergoing the *pārivāsa*, he committed another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, an intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*) similar to his previous offense, which was concealed.

The Saṃgha granted him a *mūlapārivāsa* by means of a formal act (*karma*) that was legal, irreversible, and not subject to suspension. While still undergoing that *mūlapārivāsa*, he committed yet another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, a secondary intermediate offense (*pratyantarāpatti*) similar to the intermediate offense, which was also concealed.
The Saṃgha granted him a *mūlāpakarṣa* by means of an illegal act that was both reversible and subject to suspension; it also granted him a *mānāpya* illegally,
and it also readmitted him illegally.
This person is called one who is half-black; he is impure and has not emerged from that offense, and thus is not liberated from it.
Now, another person has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and concealed it.
The Saṃgha has granted him *parivāsa* by means of a formal act (*karman*) that is in accordance with the Dharma, irreversible, and not subject to suspension.
While still undergoing the *parivāsa*, he committed another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, an intermediate offense similar to his previous one, which was concealed.

The Saṃgha granted him a *mūlaparivāsa* by means of a formal act (*karma*) that was legal, irreversible, and not subject to suspension. While still undergoing that *mūlaparivāsa*, he committed yet another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, a secondary intermediate offense similar to the intermediate offense, which was also concealed.
The Saṃgha has granted him a *mūlāpakarṣa* by means of a legal action that is irreversible and not subject to suspension; it has also granted him a *mānāpya* by means of an illegal action,
and it has also restored him by means of an illegal action.
This person is called one who has committed [the offense] for a single part and a single time; he is impure and has not emerged from it, and is therefore not liberated from that offense.
Now, there is another person who has fallen into a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that was concealed.
The Saṃgha granted him *parivāsa* by means of a formal act (*karman*) that is in accordance with the Dharma, irreversible, and not subject to suspension.
While still in the state of being one undergoing parivāsa, he committed another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, an intermediate offense similar to his previous one, which was concealed.
The Saṃgha granted him a *mūlāpakarṣa* by means of a legal, irreversible, and unobjectionable formal act (*karma*).

While still in the state of being one undergoing *mūla-parivāsa*, he committed yet another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, a subsequent intermediate offense similar to the intermediate one, which was also concealed.

The Saṃgha granted him a *mūlāpakarṣa* by means of a legal act that is irreversible and not subject to suspension; it also granted him a *mānāpya* by means of a legal act. However, he was reintegrated [from the *mānāpya*] by means of an illegal act.
This person is called one who has committed an offense for a limited time; he is impure and has not emerged from it, and is therefore not liberated from that offense.
Now, another person has fallen into a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and concealed it.
The Saṃgha has granted him *parivāsa* by means of a formal act (*karma*) that is in accordance with the Dharma, irreversible, and not subject to suspension.
While still a *pārivāsika*, he committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, an intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*) similar in nature to his previous offense, which was concealed.

The Saṃgha granted him a *mūlaparivāsa* by means of a legal act that was irreversible and not subject to suspension. While still a *mūlapārivāsika*, he committed another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, a subsequent intermediate offense (*pratyantarāpatti*) similar in nature to the intermediate offense, which was also concealed.
The Saṃgha has granted him a *mūlāpakarṣa* by means of a legal act that is irreversible and not subject to suspension; it has also granted him a *mānāpya* legally,
and it has also reintegrated him legally.
This is called a person who has removed the black stain; being pure and emerged from that offense, he is liberated from it.
Now, another person has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that was not concealed.
The Saṃgha granted him a *mānāpya* through an illegal act that is subject to censure.
While he was still in the state of performing the *mānāpya*,
he committed another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, an intermediate offense similar to his previous one, which he had concealed.
The Saṃgha granted him a *mūla-mānāpya* by means of an illegal act— one that is contested and subject to suspension.
While he was still undergoing the *mūlamānāpya*, he committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, a secondary offense similar to the previous one, which was concealed.
The Saṃgha granted him a *mūlāpakarṣamānāpya* by means of an illegal act— one that is contested and subject to suspension—
and he was also reintegrated [into the community] by an illegal act.
This is called a person who is impure at all times and has not emerged from that offense; he is not liberated from it.
Now, there is another person who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that was not concealed.
The Saṃgha granted him *mānāpya* by means of a legal act that is irreversible and not subject to suspension.
While he was still in the state of undergoing *mānāpya*, he committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, an intermediate offense similar to his previous offense, which he concealed.

The Saṃgha granted him a *mūlamānāpya* by means of an illegal act—one that is subject to censure and should be set aside. While he was still in the state of undergoing that *mūlamānāpya*, he committed another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, a subsequent intermediate offense similar to the intermediate offense, which he also concealed.

The Saṃgha granted him a *mūlāpakarṣamānāpya* by means of an illegal act—one that is reversible and subject to suspension—and he was also reintegrated [into the community] by means of an illegal act. This person is called a *yadbhūyaskālaka*; he is impure, has not emerged from his offense, and is not liberated from it.
Now, there was another person who had committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that was not concealed.
The Saṃgha granted him a *mānāpya* by means of a legal act that was irreversible and not subject to suspension.
While he was still in the state of undergoing the *mānāpya*, he committed another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense—an intermediate offense similar in nature to his previous one—which was concealed.

The Saṃgha granted him a *mūlamānāpya* by means of a legal, irreversible, and non-settling procedure. While he was still in the state of performing the *mūlamānāpya*, he committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that was similar to the intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*), namely a subsequent offense (*pratyantarāpatti*), which he concealed.

The Saṃgha granted him a *mūlāpakarṣamānāpya* by means of an illegal act—one that is reversible and subject to being set aside—and he was also reintegrated [into the community] by means of an illegal act. This person is called one who is "half-black"; he is impure, has not emerged from his offense, and is not liberated from it.
Now, there was another person who had committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that was not concealed.
The Saṃgha granted him a *mānāpya* by means of a legal, irreversible, and non-settling formal act (*karma*).
While he was still in the state of performing the *mānāpya*, he committed another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense—an intermediate offense similar to his previous one—which was concealed.
The Saṃgha granted him a *mūlamānāpya* by means of a legal, irreversible, and non-settling formal act (*karma*).
While he was still undergoing that *mūlamānāpya*, he committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, a secondary offense similar to the intermediate offense, which was concealed.
The Saṃgha granted him a *mūlāpakarṣamānāpya* by means of a legal, irreversible, and non-settling formal act.

But one who has been reintegrated through an illegal procedure is called a person who is "partially and temporarily" [rehabilitated]; he is impure, not emerged from that offense, and is not liberated from it.
Now, there is another person who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that was not concealed.
The Saṃgha granted him a *mānāpya* by means of a legal, irreversible, and unobjectionable formal act.
While he was still in the state of performing the *mānāpya*, he committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, an intermediate offense similar to his previous one, which he had concealed.
The Saṃgha granted him a fundamental *mānāpya* (*mūlamānāpya*) by means of a legal, irreversible, and unobjectionable formal act.
While he was still in the state of one undergoing *mūlamānāpya*, he committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, a secondary offense (*pratyantarāpatti*) similar to the previous offense, which was concealed.
The Saṃgha granted him a *mūlāpakarṣamānāpya* by means of a legal, irreversible, and non-settling procedure;
it was also [formally] revoked by a legal procedure.
This person is called one who has removed the black stain; being pure and emerged from that offense, he is liberated from it.
Two persons have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and say, "We shall confess, we shall confess. Therein, one confesses while the second does not confess.

In that case, for one who does not confess, after he has confessed numerous offenses involving a violation of the Vinaya and grave transgressions (*duṣṭhula*), probation (*parivāsa*) must subsequently be granted, as well as initial probation (*mūlaparivāsa*) and penance (*mānāpya*).
He is also to be reintegrated into the community (*āvarhitavya*).
Two individuals have fallen into an offense entailing formal meeting of the Saṃgha (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*).
"We two shall confess [our offenses] right here in this very residence in the presence of a person; we shall confess.
There, one confesses while the second does not confess.

In that case, after that one who did not confess has been made to confess many offenses that violate the Vinaya and are *duṣṭhula*, probation (*parivāsa*) should subsequently be granted, as well as initial probation (*mūlaparivāsa*) and penance (*mānāpya*).
And he must be expelled.
Just as it is toward one person, so it is toward two, toward many, or toward the Saṃgha;
just as it is in this residence, so it is in another residence.
Now, another person commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and conceals it.
The Saṃgha grants him *parivāsa* by means of an illegal act—one that is contested and subject to suspension.
While he is still in the state of *pārivāsika*, he becomes aware of another offense which he has not disclosed in the midst of the Saṃgha.
He knows that offense;
he also knows that offense which was not announced in the midst of the Saṃgha by means of a vehicle.
He announces it to the monks.
"Venerable sirs, I have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that was concealed.

The Saṃgha granted me *parivāsa* by means of an illegal act—one that is contested and subject to suspension. While I was still in the state of being one undergoing *parivāsa*, I committed another offense."
"I know that which I did not disclose in the midst of the Saṃgha;
yet I do not recognize that offense for which the Saṃgha granted me *parivāsa* by means of an illegal act—one that is contested and subject to suspension.
It would be well, venerable sirs, if you would grant me *parivāsa* even for that previous offense by means of a legal act—one that is uncontested and not subject to suspension."
And regarding this later offense,

those monks grant him *parivāsa* for that earlier offense by means of a legal act that is irreversible and not subject to suspension; yet they grant *parivāsa* for that later offense by means of an illegal act that is reversible and subject to suspension.

While still in the state of being one undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*), he committed another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, an intermediate offense similar in form to his previous offense, which was concealed.
He recognizes that intermediate offense;
he also recognizes the offense for which the Saṃgha granted him probation by means of an illegal act—one that is contested and subject to suspension.
He informs the monks:
"Venerable sirs, I have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that was concealed.
The Saṃgha has granted me *parivāsa* by means of an illegal act—one that is contested and subject to suspension."
While still a *pārivāsika*, I committed another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, an intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*) similar to my previous one, which was concealed.
I recognize that intermediate offense for which the Saṃgha granted me a *parivāsa* by means of an illegal act—one that is contested and subject to suspension.
Venerable sirs, please kindly grant me a *mūlaparivāsa* for that previous offense according to the Dharma.
"By means of a formal act that is irreversible, unshakeable, and not subject to being set aside;
and for that intermediate offense, a *mūlaparivāsa* (fundamental probation).
O monks, they grant him probation for that previous offense by means of a formal act that is in accordance with the Dharma, irreversible, and not subject to being set aside."
But for that intermediate offense, he was granted a *mūlaparivāsa* by means of an illegal act— one that is reversible and subject to being set aside.
While he was still in the state of a *mūlapārivāsika*, he committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, a secondary offense similar to the intermediate offense, which was concealed.
He recognizes that intermediate offense,
and he also recognizes the offense for which the Saṃgha had granted him a *mūlaparivāsa* by means of an illegal action— one that is contested and subject to suspension.
He then informs the monks.

"Venerable sirs, I have fallen into a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that is a subsequent offense similar to a previous offense, and it was concealed. The Saṃgha granted me a *mūlaparivāsa* by means of a legal, irreversible, and non-settling formal act (*karma*). While I was still in the state of being a *mūlapārivāsika*, I fell into another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, a re-occurrence similar to the intermediate offense, which was also concealed."
Thus, I recognize that intermediate offense;
I also recognize that very intermediate offense for which the Saṃgha granted me a *mūlaparivāsa* by means of an illegal act—one that is contested and subject to suspension.
Venerable sirs, it would be well if you would grant me a *mūlaparivāsa* for that intermediate offense by means of a legal act—one that is uncontested and not subject to suspension.
"And regarding this secondary offense, there is a 'renewed reduction from the root' (mūlāpakarṣa).
Those monks grant him a *mūlaparivāsa* for that previous offense,
but a *mūlāpakarṣa* for this secondary offense by means of a formal act (*karma*) that is lawful, irreversible, and not subject to suspension.
Now, another person commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that was not concealed.
The Saṃgha grants him a *mānāpya* by means of an illegal act—one that is contested and subject to suspension.
While he is still merely in the state of performing the *mānāpya*, he commits another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, an intermediate offense similar to his previous one, which was also not concealed.
He recognizes that intermediate offense for which the Saṃgha had granted him *mānāpya* by means of an illegal act— one that is contested and subject to suspension—
and he informs the monks.
Venerable sirs, I have fallen into a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that was not concealed.

The Saṃgha granted me *mānāpya* by means of an illegal act—one that is contested and subject to suspension. While I was still in the state of being a *mānāpyacārika*, I fell into another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, an intermediate offense similar in form to my previous offense, which was also not concealed.
"I know that intermediate offense for which the Saṃgha granted me a *mānāpya* by means of an illegal act— one that is contested and subject to suspension.

Venerable sirs, please grant me a *mānāpya* for that previous offense by means of a legal act that is uncontested and not subject to suspension, and grant me a *mūlamānāpya* for this intermediate offense."
Monks, they grant him a *mānāpya* for that previous offense by means of a legal act that is irreversible and not subject to suspension;
however, they grant a *mūlamānāpya* for this intervening offense by means of an illegal act that is reversible and subject to suspension.
While he is still undergoing that very *mūlamānāpya*, he commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, a subsequent offense similar to the intervening offense, which was not concealed.
He recognizes that intermediate offense;
he also recognizes that very intermediate offense for which the Saṃgha has granted him a *mūlamānāpya* by means of an illegal act—one that is contested and subject to suspension.
He informs the monks.
Venerable sirs, I have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that is similar to a previous offense, namely an intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*), which was not concealed.
The Saṃgha has granted me a *mūlamānāpya* by means of an illegal act— one that is contested and subject to suspension.

While I was still undergoing the *mūlamānāpya*, I committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, a secondary offense (*pratyantarāpatti*) similar to the intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*), which was unconfessed. I recognize that secondary offense,
and I also recognize that intermediate offense for which the Saṃgha granted me a *mūlamānāpya* by means of an illegal act— one that is contested and subject to suspension.

"Excellent, excellent, venerable ones! Grant for that previous intermediate offense a *mūlamānāpya* by means of a legal action that is irreversible and not subject to suspension; and for this subsequent intermediate offense, grant a *mūlāpakarṣamānāpya*."
Monks, they grant him a *mūlamānāpya* for that previous intermediate offense by means of a legal act that is irreversible and not subject to suspension;
and they grant a *mūlāpakarṣamānāpya* for this subsequent intermediate offense.
Just as there are five [cases] for one who knows, so there are five for one who remembers, and five for one who is in doubt.
The summary verse:
Just as the twelvefold [section] follows, so too the sixfold [section] after the subject matter has been cleared;
and having cleared the Great Section (mahābhūmi), the subject matter of the person (pudgalavastu) is fully set forth.
Now, another person commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and conceals it.
The Saṃgha grants him *parivāsa* by means of an illegal act—one that is contested and subject to suspension.
While he is still in the state of being a *pārivāsika*, he commits another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, an intermediate offense similar in form to his previous one, which he also conceals.
He recognizes that intermediate offense;
he also recognizes that very offense for which the Saṃgha granted him probation by means of an illegal act— one that is contested and subject to suspension—
and he informs the monks.
Venerable sirs, I have fallen into a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense which was concealed.

The Saṃgha granted me *parivāsa* by means of an illegal act—one that is contested and subject to suspension. While I was still in the state of being one undergoing *parivāsa*, I fell into another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, an intermediate offense similar to my previous offense, which was also concealed.
Thus, I recognize that intermediate offense;
I also recognize that offense for which the Saṃgha granted me *parivāsa* by means of an illegal act—one that is contested and subject to suspension.
Venerable sirs, please grant me *parivāsa* for that previous offense by means of a legal act, one that is uncontested and not subject to suspension.
"And regarding that intermediate offense, there is a *mūlaparivāsa*.
Those monks grant him *parivāsa* for that previous offense by means of a legal act (*dharmakarma*) that is irreversible and not subject to suspension;
however, they grant him *mūlaparivāsa* for this intermediate offense by means of an illegal act (*adharmakarma*) that is reversible and subject to suspension.

While still in the state of being a *mūlapārivāsika*, he committed another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, a secondary offense (*pratyantarāpatti*) similar to the previous intermediate offense, which was concealed. He recognizes that secondary offense,
and he also recognizes the intermediate offense for which the Saṃgha had granted him the *mūlaparivāsa* by means of an illegal act— one that is contested and subject to suspension.
He informs the monks:
"Venerable sirs, I have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that is a subsequent offense identical in form to a previous offense, and it was concealed.
The Saṃgha granted me a *mūlaparivāsa* by means of an illegal act—one that is contested and subject to suspension."
While still a *mūlapārivāsika*, I committed another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, a subsequent offense similar to the previous one, which was concealed. I recognize that subsequent offense;
I also recognize that intermediate offense.

"Venerable sirs, the Sangha has granted me a *mūlaparivāsa* for that previous offense by means of an illegal act— one that is reversible and subject to being set aside. It would be well if the venerable ones would grant me a *mūlaparivāsa* for that same previous offense by means of a legal act— one that is irreversible and not subject to being set aside— and a *mūlāpakarṣa* for this subsequent offense."
Monks, they grant him a *mūlaparivāsa* for that previous intermediate offense by means of a legal act that is irreversible and not subject to suspension;
and they grant him a *mūlāpakarṣa* for that subsequent intermediate offense by means of a legal act that is irreversible and not subject to suspension.
Now, suppose another person has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that was not concealed.

The Saṃgha granted him a mānāpya by means of an illegal act that was contested and subject to suspension. While he was still in the state of performing the mānāpya, he committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense,
an intermediate offense similar to his previous one, which was not concealed.
He knows that intermediate offense;
he also knows that very offense for which the Saṃgha granted him a *mānāpya* by means of an illegal act—one that is contested and subject to suspension. He informs the monks.
Venerable sirs, I have fallen into a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that was not concealed.
The Saṃgha granted me a six-night *mānāpya* by means of an illegal act—one that is contested and subject to suspension.
While I was still in the state of performing the *mānāpya*, I fell into another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, an intermediate offense similar to my previous one, which was also not concealed.
Thus, I recognize that intermediate offense;

I also recognize that offense for which the Saṃgha granted me a *mānāpya* by means of an illegal act—one that is contested and subject to suspension. Venerable sirs, please grant me a *mānāpya* for that previous offense by means of a legal act, one that is uncontested and not subject to suspension.

"And for this intermediate offense, there is a *mūlamānāpya* (root probation). Thus, those monks grant him *mānāpya* for that previous offense by means of a legal act that is irreversible and not subject to suspension;
but they grant a *mūlamānāpya* for this intermediate offense by means of an illegal act that is reversible and subject to suspension.

While he was still in the state of undergoing *mūla-mānāpya*, he committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, a secondary offense (*pratyantarāpatti*) similar to the previous offense (*antarāpatti*), which was unconfessed. He knew that secondary offense,
and he also knew the previous offense for which the Saṃgha had granted him *mūla-mānāpya* by means of an illegal act— one that is contested and subject to suspension.
He informs the monks:
"Venerable sirs, I have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that is similar to a previous offense, namely an intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*), which was not concealed.
The Saṃgha has granted me a *mūlamānāpya* by means of an illegal act—one that is contested and subject to suspension."
While I was still undergoing the *mūlamānāpya* penance, I committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense—
a secondary offense (*pratyantarāpatti*) similar to the intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*), which was unconfessed.
I am aware of that secondary offense.
"I also recognize that intermediate offense for which the Saṃgha granted me a *mūlamānāpya* by means of an illegal act— one that is contested and subject to suspension.
Venerable sirs, it would be well if you were to grant me a *mūlamānāpya* for that previous intermediate offense by means of a legal act— one that is uncontested and not subject to suspension—
and a *mūlāpakarṣamānāpya* for this subsequent intermediate offense."

Monks, they grant him a *mūlamānāpya* for that previous intermediate offense by means of a legal act that is irreversible and not subject to suspension; but for this subsequent intermediate offense, they grant a *mūlāpakarṣamānāpya*.
Just as there are four cases for one who knows, so too there are four for one who remembers, and four for one who is in doubt.
A person undergoing probation committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One,
and the Blessed One said:
Having cleared the matter and confessed a grave offense (*duṣṭhula*) that constitutes a transgression of the discipline, while still being one who is undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*),
a person who has completed half of his probation commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
The monks report this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Having cleared away the matter and confessed the *duṣṭhula* offense that constitutes a transgression of the Vinaya, while still being one who has undergone only half of the *parivāsa*,
that person— being one who has undergone more than half of the *parivāsa*— incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Having cleared the matter and confessed the grave offense (*duṣṭhulā*) that constitutes a transgression of the Vinaya, he remains for the most part still a *pārivāsika*."
A person undergoing the *mānāpya* penance committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
Having cleared the matter and confessed the *duṣṭhula* offense that constituted a transgression of the discipline, while still in the process of performing the *mānāpya*,
a person who was in the midst of performing half of the *mānāpya* committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
Having purified the matter and confessed the *duṣṭhula* offense that constitutes a transgression of the Vinaya, while still in the state of undergoing half of the *mānāpya*,
a person who was already undergoing more than half of the *mānāpya* commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Having cleared the matter and having confessed the offense of *duṣṭhula* which transgresses the Vinaya, while still being one who is undergoing the *yadbhūyomānāpya* penance."
Now, another person commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense arising from intentional emission of semen, concealed for one night;
an offense arising from grasping, concealed for two nights;
and an offense arising from lewd conversation, concealed for three nights.
[The offense] arising from personal service, concealed for four nights;
[the offense] arising from acting as a go-between, concealed for five nights;
[the offense] arising from building a small hut, concealed for six nights.
[The offense] arising from [accusing a monk of being] aged, concealed for seven nights;
that arising from [accusing him of] groundless [charges], concealed for eight nights;
and that arising from [accusing him of] a minor [offense], concealed for nine nights.
[The offense] arising from causing a schism in the Saṃgha, concealed for ten nights;
that arising from following after [the schismatic], concealed for eleven nights;
and that arising from corrupting families, concealed for twelve nights.
[The offense] arising from harsh speech, concealed for thirteen nights.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

Whatever severity, gravity, or intensity of obsession characterizes these offenses, probation (parivāsa) must be granted according to that; likewise, initial probation (mūlaparivāsa), reduction from the beginning (mūlāpakarṣa), penance (mānāpya), and reinstatement (āvarhaṇa) must be administered.
The section on persons (pudgalavastu) is concluded.
